source: Glucksberg (1962), as summarised in Wikipedia 'Candle problem'
finding: Candle problem in a 2x2 design: tacks and matches either inside or outside their boxes, with or without cash prizes. The empty-box (objects outside boxes) version was easier than the filled-box version.
numbers: Prizes: none (low drive), $5 for the top 25%, $20 for the best (high drive). N not given in the secondary source.
limits: Secondary source only; primary paper not opened. No sample sizes available here.
agent_relevance: Fixation is manipulable by how objects are presented. An S1 restatement that detaches objects from their packaging (name the parts) mirrors the free-box manipulation.

source: Glucksberg (1962) incentive result, via Wikipedia 'Candle problem'
finding: Within the filled-box condition, high-drive (prize) subjects did worse than low-drive subjects. Pressure made fixation worse, not better.
numbers: Direction only: high drive worse than low drive in the filled-box condition. Wikipedia gives no N or means.
quote: high drive prolongs extinction of the dominant habit and thus retards the correct habit from gaining ascendancy
limits: Often over-generalised to 'incentives hurt creativity'. It applies where the dominant habit is wrong. Popular retellings are not a replication. No replication was found or opened this session.
agent_relevance: Do not raise urgency or stakes in the prompt when the problem is a fixation trap. Fits G1: pressure strengthens the dominant habit.

source: Adamson (1952) candle-box repetition, via Wikipedia 'Functional fixedness'
finding: A repetition of Duncker-style experiments: people shown an empty tack box were about twice as likely to solve as people shown the box filled with tacks.
numbers: Ratio about 2:1 (empty vs filled). N not stated in the secondary source.
limits: Secondary source. It does not say whether all three repeated experiments held up. Counts as an early direct replication of Duncker's pre-utilisation effect.
agent_relevance: Supports O6-style relabelling: remove the object from its habitual frame and the solve rate roughly doubles.

source: Frank & Ramscar (2003) written candle problem, via Wikipedia 'Functional fixedness' and 'Candle problem'
finding: Wording and typography change fixation. Underlining noun phrases such as 'box of matches' raised solving from 23% to 55%. Underlining only the nouns gave 47%.
numbers: Stanford undergraduates, written version: 23% baseline vs 55% (phrases) vs 47% (nouns). The Candle problem page says 25% to 50%, a small mismatch between two Wikipedia pages.
limits: Secondary source; N not given. The two pages disagree on the baseline (23 vs 25 percent), so check the primary before citing a point value.
agent_relevance: How the problem text names objects is a lever. A restatement step that separates 'box' from 'box of tacks' is a cheap operator.

source: McCaffrey (2012) generic-parts technique, via Wikipedia 'Functional fixedness'
finding: Training people to break objects into parts and describe each part without its use (generic parts technique) reduced fixedness.
numbers: Trained people solved 67% more fixedness-affected problems than a control group.
limits: Relative gain, not absolute rates. No N in the secondary source. Primary and any independent replication not opened. Patrick & Ahmed (2014, via Tran review) also report a representation-change training benefit.
agent_relevance: Best-supported intervention for S1/O6: list parts of each object in neutral terms (material, shape, size) before proposing uses. Easy to test on an LLM.

source: Tran, Esseily, Bovet & Kiraly (2021) review: mutual exclusivity in tool use learning
finding: Development of fixedness: 6- and 7-year-olds, but not 5-year-olds, struggle to use objects in unconventional ways (German & Defeyter 2000). Four-year-olds show none after an adult demonstration (Nielsen 2012). Fixedness follows learned function.
numbers: Ages only: 5 yr no effect; 6-7 yr effect; 4 yr no fixedness after demonstration. The review gives no N or percentages.
limits: First 100k characters of the page read; last 15.6k not read. Competing view: older children may do better through innovation, not through resisting fixedness.
agent_relevance: Fixedness grows with learned function. A model with many documented uses per object may be more fixated, not less.

source: Tran et al. (2021) review: moderators of fixedness in adults and children
finding: Moderators: priming an object's main function raises fixation (Camarda 2018, higher EEG alpha); high-fixedness objects (a desktop) give fewer alternative uses than low-fixedness ones (a blanket) (Kroneisen 2021); learning modality (read, watch, manipulate) did not matter (Munoz-Rubke 2018); an in-group demonstrator changed 4-year-olds' tool choice, an out-group one did not (Peto 2018).
numbers: No numbers in the review text. All cited studies unopened.
limits: Secondary summary of four separate studies; effect sizes unknown.
agent_relevance: Priming an object's habitual use, even by describing it, can deepen fixation. A prompt that lists 'what X is normally for' before asking for new uses could backfire.

source: German & Barrett (2005) Shuar functional fixedness, via Wikipedia and Tran review
finding: Shuar adults of Ecuador (low-tech culture) also showed functional fixedness: slower to pick materials in the box task and slower on a spoon task, with no difference in solve time on the box task.
numbers: No percentages or N in either secondary source.
limits: Called 'preliminary evidence' of universality. No replication reported in these sources. Primary paper not opened (publisher returned 403).
agent_relevance: Fixedness is not an artefact of Western tool culture, so it is plausibly a general property of any system with strong function priors.

source: Hanus et al. (2011) and Ebel et al. (2021) apes, via Tran review
finding: Apes show fixedness too. Chimpanzees struggled with a familiar water dispenser in the floating-peanut task and did better with a novel one. Great apes that had eaten grissini used it less as a rake than naive apes.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Secondary summary. Lab apes with partly unknown tool histories.
agent_relevance: Experience with the habitual use blocks the new use, the same Gestalt claim in another species.

source: Functional fixedness in chimpanzees (2024), Study 1
finding: Chimpanzees given 5 drinking sessions with a tool were slower to use it for a new function than controls, and the effect held 9 months later.
numbers: 16 chimpanzees (mean age 23). Time to success: group chi2(1)=7.33, p=0.007. Time to extract target tool: chi2(1)=8.26, p=0.004. Task success: experience 5/8 vs control 8/8, Fisher p=0.200. Sucking at the dry hose: 6/8 vs 1/8, p=0.041.
limits: Small sample, one population, no pilot, floor effects. The difference in final success was not significant; the difference was in speed.
agent_relevance: Fixedness often shows as delay rather than failure. Measure steps or tokens to the first valid reframe, not only final accuracy.

source: Functional fixedness in chimpanzees (2024), Study 2 (observation only)
finding: Watching a demonstrator use a tool for its usual function gave only tentative evidence of fixation. Only 2 of 14 chimpanzees (both controls) used the straw to retrieve the reward.
numbers: 14 chimpanzees. Finding the solution strategy: chi2(1)=5.23, p=0.022. Time to find it: p=0.066 (trend). Target tool selection: 2/7 vs 3/7, p=0.576. The sucking-at-straw line repeats the same statistic and may be a reporting error.
limits: Floor effect. Possible carry-over from Study 1. Authors call the evidence tentative.
agent_relevance: Seeing a function demonstrated (an in-context example) is a weaker cause of fixation than hands-on use. May matter for few-shot prompts.

source: The detour paradigm in animal cognition (2018 review)
finding: Review of at least 127 studies on 96 species. Kohler (1925) used detours to probe insight. Dogs that had used a detour many times kept using it when a shortcut opened (called functional fixedness). A 'knowing/acting mismatch' exists: the visible goal pulls the animal to the barrier.
numbers: Cylinder task on 36 species (29 mammals, 7 birds); great apes best, three corvid species matched apes. Chickens in Thorndike's work ignored later shortcuts after about 75-80 trials.
limits: Authors report little agreement on what a detour requires; rearing, motivation and barrier material confound results. Text beyond 100k characters not read.
agent_relevance: Separate 'cannot see the new route' from 'sees it but repeats the habitual move'. Code-side blocking of repeated failed actions handles the second; S1 renaming handles the first.

source: Luchins (1942) water jar Einstellung, via Wikipedia 'Einstellung effect'
finding: Practice with a fixed method made children keep using it when a simpler method existed. Stress raised the effect.
numbers: 483 children aged 9-12. Non-stress: 70% rigid on test problems, 58% failed the extinction problem. Anxiety condition: 98% and 97%. Speed test, one class: only 3 of 98 solved the extinction problem.
limits: Secondary source. 1942 methods, no modern power analysis. No replication numbers opened here.
agent_relevance: Practice on a working method is itself a fixation source. Few-shot examples that all share one solution path are the LLM version of the practice set.

source: Luchins & Luchins (1959) and age studies, via Wikipedia 'Einstellung effect'
finding: Einstellung was not tied to IQ, and it rose with age and anxiety. Intelligence did not protect.
numbers: IQ link not significant; IQ ranges 51-160 (showed effect) vs 75-155 (did not). Extinction task: 56% young adults, 68% children, 69% older adults. Ross 1952: 65% of older adults (mean 60.8) failed vs 29% of middle-aged (37.3).
limits: Secondary source; cross-sectional; N given only for Luchins' groups (140 children, 79 students, 21 adults).
agent_relevance: General ability alone does not remove fixation, which argues for a structural operator (O6) rather than 'think harder'.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) Einstellung in chess: choices
finding: Replicated the Bilalic finding that a familiar solution draws attention and blocks a better one. On a problem where the familiar move was good but not best, experts and novices fell in equally.
numbers: 34 players (17 experts, mean rating 2223; 17 novices). Problem 1: 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose the Einstellung move; 9 experts found the optimal move. 4 experimental problems plus 8 fillers, 3 min each.
limits: Small N. The effect was weak when the familiar move was a blunder (Problems 2-4): all experts and most novices avoided it. Authors suggest feedback from a refuted move restarts search.
agent_relevance: The trap is strongest when the habitual answer is good enough. The check should fire on 'plausible and passes visible tests', not only on obvious failure (G3).

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) Einstellung in chess: mechanism
finding: Mechanism is biased attention to features of the first idea, not lack of ability. Dwell count separated continued search of the familiar move from returning to the better region; looking time alone overstated fixation.
numbers: First fixation on target region: experts 407 ms vs novices 719 ms. Optimal-move experts (n=9) had more dwells than Einstellung-move experts, F(1,15)=12.34, p<.01, and than novices, F(1,15)=13.46, p<.01. Bilalic et al. (2008) reported experts with a familiar solution fell to the level of players about 3 SD weaker (as cited).
limits: Eye movements are a proxy. The 3 SD figure is cited, not re-derived; Bilalic 2008 not opened.
agent_relevance: Count revisits to alternatives, not time spent. Suggests a code-side impasse metric: number of distinct frames tried, not tokens spent.

source: Ellis & Reingold (2014) Einstellung in anagram solving
finding: Familiar-word central strings slowed solving but did not lower accuracy. Unlike chess, no attentional bias to the familiar string was found; authors favour involuntary activation of the familiar word.
numbers: 60 students, 72 trials, 45 s limit. Accuracy 51.7% (word) vs 53.8% (nonword), n.s. Correct RT 15.3 s vs 13.4 s, t(59)=3.25, p<0.01. Dwells on central string 8.11 vs 6.76. Overall 52.7% correct, 43.1% timeouts.
limits: Mechanism not directly tested. Three-letter central strings only. Cost was speed, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Not all fixation is an attention trap. Some is automatic activation that cannot be suppressed, so naming the distractor may not remove it; a different frame is needed.

source: Huang, Tang & Hu (2018) short-term mental set in chunk decomposition
finding: More practice with one solution type made the other, harder-to-see type slower and, in Exp 1, less accurate. The set persisted even when the test problem looked different.
numbers: Exp 1: 32 participants, accuracy interaction F(1,31)=11.00, p=0.002, eta2=0.26; RT interaction eta2=0.16. Exp 2: 28 participants, RT interaction F(1,27)=29.50, eta2=0.52; accuracy unaffected. Practice 156 vs 24 problems.
limits: Chinese character task, undergraduates. One reported t(31)=9.42, p=0.004 is internally inconsistent (probable typo).
agent_relevance: Set strength scales with how often the first method was reinforced. An agent that has solved N similar items in context should treat the (N+1)th as suspect.

source: Incubation meta-analyses and moderators (Sio & Ormerod 2009; Strick 2011), in a 2016 review
finding: Breaks help, modestly. Benefit is larger when the interpolated task is undemanding than when it is demanding or absent.
numbers: Sio & Ormerod (2009): 117 studies, mean d=0.29. Strick et al. (2011): 92 decision studies, g=0.224. Segal (2004): 4 and 12 minute breaks helped equally.
limits: Mixed insight and divergent tasks. Smith & Blankenship (1991) and Vul & Pashler not covered in this text. Effects are low-medium and heterogeneous.
agent_relevance: A forced pause is a weak lever. Consistent with G1: do not schedule rethinking, and expect small gains from any 'step away' operator.

source: Beneficial forgetting (Smith 1995; Segal 2004), in the same 2016 review
finding: Fixation fades as misleading cues are forgotten: with word problems, solving became more likely as participants forgot the cues, and forgetting grew with break length.
numbers: No numbers reported in this review for Smith (1995).
limits: Secondary. Review does not mention Vul & Pashler's misled-incubation result.
agent_relevance: The LLM analogue of forgetting is dropping failed attempts from context before retrying. Testable: retry from a clean context holding only the check outcome.

source: Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (2020)
finding: The context of attempt changes solving, and switching context after an impasse helped. In the necklace problem, high-interactivity presentation solved far more than low.
numbers: Exp 1, N=63: Time 1 43% (12/28) vs 6% (2/35), chi2=12.42, p<.001. Exp 2, N=61: low-to-high switch 61% (14/23) of earlier non-solvers vs high-to-low 5% (1/20); low-to-low 15%. Gains: low-to-high +52%, high-to-low +3%.
limits: No no-break control. Small cells (Fisher tests), mostly female psychology students, N reported inconsistently (61 vs 55/56). One problem, 2-week gap.
agent_relevance: Changing the representation context after failure beat repeating it, matching O6. A reframe operator should change the presentation, not just retry.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem
finding: Problem type does not fix the process. Classic insight problems, non-insight problems and compound remote associates all produced both insight-like and step-by-step solving.
numbers: Exp 1 N=193, Exp 1a N=82, Exp 2 N=129. Accuracy: insight 0.51/0.49/0.45, non-insight 0.54/0.64/0.56. Aha-accuracy r for insight 0.50/0.40/0.495; for non-insight 0.02/0.24/0.19.
limits: Self-reported Aha only. Some table values conflict with the text (Exp 1a). Melbourne students only.
agent_relevance: Do not build a special 'insight mode'. Treat fixation as one failure type inside the ordinary loop, triggered by check failure, not by problem label.

source: Tian et al. MacGyver: Are LLMs creative problem solvers? headline results
finding: 1,683 verbal problems built to push against functional fixedness. In single attempts LLMs fell well short of people; on majority vote the gap was small.
numbers: Seven LLMs: 35% to 42% single-attempt success; average person 65.1%. Majority: humans 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Over 82% of solvable problems need unconventional tool use.
limits: Humans: one random response per problem. Problems generated with LLM help. Models are 2023 vintage (GPT-3.5, GPT-4-0613, Llama2, Claude2, PaLM2).
agent_relevance: Direct benchmark for S1/O6 on object fixation; needs a re-run with 2026 reasoning models.

source: MacGyver error analysis of GPT-4
finding: LLM failure is mostly infeasible actions, not blind repetition of the usual use. Loosening the habitual use creates new errors about affordances.
numbers: Error shares (Table 2 reading order): wrong tool usage 42.4%; not achieving the goal 17.7%; using unavailable tools 16.9%; wrong spatial understanding 10.8%; ignoring constraints 9.5%. A solution can have more than one error.
limits: PDF table layout is garbled, so the mapping of the lower rows to percentages may be off.
agent_relevance: Check feasibility with code or a simulator where possible; reframing needs a G2/G3 check.

source: MacGyver prompting interventions
finding: Two zero-shot methods helped GPT-4. Self-reflection cut infeasible solutions more; divergent-then-convergent thinking raised efficient solutions more.
numbers: 180 solvable problems, GPT-4. Infeasible solutions: Self-Reflect -9.7 points vs Div-Conv -4.3. Efficient solutions: Div-Conv +6.5 vs Self-Reflect +2.2. Claude2 and Llama2-13b did not improve with Self-Reflect; Div-Conv helped all three.
limits: Single run, 180 problems, no confidence intervals. The reflection is model-judged, which G2 and G5 distrust.
agent_relevance: Divergent-then-convergent is supported across three models, matching generate-then-select with code doing the selection.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are fixated by red herrings: Only Connect Wall
finding: A quiz-show task with deliberate red herrings serves as a fixation test. GPT-4 beat embedding baselines by more than 2x on solved walls and correct groups but stayed far below humans. Removing red herrings helped.
numbers: 618 walls from 15 seasons; human connection accuracy about 80%. Ablation sets OCW-Randomized and OCW-WordNet: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 'increased significantly' as herrings were removed. More in-context examples (1 to 10 shot) did not help.
limits: Table 5 values were not recoverable from the PDF text, so only direction is recorded. The Einstellung link rests on the ablation design, not a human control.
agent_relevance: In-context examples did not rescue fixation, which favours a structural operator over more demonstrations.

source: Kim et al. (2025) M-ARC: Einstellung in medical reasoning
finding: 100 hand-built clinical questions where a learned pattern leads wrong. Most LLMs failed, including o1 and Gemini, and showed overconfidence.
numbers: Most LLMs below 50% accuracy; several at or below 20%. Physician mean 66% (5 physicians, SE 5.3%). 100 questions.
limits: Small, adversarial benchmark, five physicians.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence on trap items means self-reported confidence cannot gate the reframe step (G5, G6).

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility (mARC follow-up)
finding: Strong reasoning models avoided Einstellung traps about as often as physicians. Reasoning mode closed the gap that non-reasoning versions left.
numbers: Claude 4.1 Opus mean 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763) vs physicians 0.66 (CI 0.55-0.75). No significant gap to humans for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning at highest reasoning effort. On questions physicians missed most, top 5 models scored 55%-70%.
limits: Same 100-question set, public since 2025, so contamination is possible. Highest reasoning effort only.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold must beat a plain reasoning-mode baseline, not a non-reasoning one.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Einstellung bias in 17 medical LLMs
finding: Paired control and trap cases show models give the common diagnosis even when evidence flips it. Better baseline accuracy did not mean fewer traps. Debate-style agent frameworks did not fix it.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. GPT-5 baseline accuracy 54.30%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.58%, bias trap rates above 50%. MDAgent and DyLAN: robust accuracy about 8-10%. Authors' ECR-Agent on Qwen3-32B: base 69.49%, robust 24.21%, trap rate 33.75%.
limits: Cases partly LLM-generated and filtered by LLM judges plus 4 physicians (kappa 0.79). Authors' own method, no outside replication.
agent_relevance: Consensus among samples can lock in the prior (G4). Gains came from checking evidence against the case, not from voting.

source: Liu, Karimnazarov & White (2025) Functional fixedness in LLM-enabled chat search
finding: Fixedness on the user side: people carry habits from search engines and assistants into chat and prompt in expected ways; unmet expectations push them to vary prompts.
numbers: 450 crowdsourced participants, six decision tasks, multi-prompt conversations with ChatGPT.
limits: Only the abstract-level findings were read in detail. Human-side study; says nothing about model fixation.
agent_relevance: Marginal: the prompt author is also fixated, so a prompt should not presuppose the habitual use.

source: Wikipedia 'Insight': Kohler and sleep/break items
finding: Kohler's apes failed repeatedly then acted purposefully, read as insight rather than trial and error. Sleep after training roughly doubled insight solutions (Wagner 2004).
numbers: Wagner 2004: sleep group about 2x the insight solutions of the awake group. Segal 2004: 4 and 12 minute breaks equal. Almost 20% of an Australian sample never experienced insight.
limits: Secondary; no replication or Weisberg critique on the page. Wagner's sleep result is single-lab and not opened.
agent_relevance: Low relevance for LLMs; relief from fixation seems to need a change of state, not elapsed time.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Einstellung in chess experts (not opened)
finding: Experts with a familiar but worse solution available played at a lower level; eye tracking showed they kept looking at the familiar route while saying they were searching.
numbers: About 3 SD drop in level, as cited by Sheridan & Reingold; not verified in the primary.
limits: Not opened; publisher blocks automated fetch. Details come from the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Self-reports of 'still searching' are unreliable, so the impasse detector should use behaviour counts (G2).

source: Vul & Pashler (2007) Incubation benefits only after people have been misled (not opened)
finding: Claim as I recall it: a break helped only when people had been given misleading hints, so the benefit is relief from fixation, not general mulling. Unverified.
numbers: Not verified this session; numbers withheld.
limits: Not opened; host unreachable. Treat as unverified recall.
agent_relevance: If true, rest or restart operators pay off only after a fixating context, supporting G1.

source: Birch (1945) experience and ape tool use (not opened)
finding: Claim as I recall it: young chimpanzees without prior stick play often failed Kohler-style tasks, so prior experience supplies the 'insight'. Unverified.
numbers: Not verified this session; numbers withheld.
limits: Not opened. Recall pointer for the next pass.
agent_relevance: Insight may be recombination of stored experience. For an LLM the needed use is in the weights and retrieval is the problem.
